planting.note: Plant container-grown rooted cuttings in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; 'Hercules' is a male-flowering selection bred at the University of Connecticut specifically to pollinate female American bittersweet vines such as 'Diana' -- plant one 'Hercules' within 20-30 feet of several females to guarantee reliable fruit set since straight-species seedlings are unpredictably male or female.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade on a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor. 'Hercules' was selected and introduced by the University of Connecticut's woody plant breeding program specifically to solve the frustration of growing seed-grown American bittersweet, which is dioecious and produces no berries roughly half the time because the seedling turns out male; 'Hercules' is a vigorous, reliably male clone bred purely as a pollen source, with the same twining habit and small, inconspicuous early-summer flowers as the species but no ornamental fruit of its own. Pair it with the female clone 'Diana' or other known female bittersweet for dependable, heavy orange-and-scarlet fall and winter fruit clusters on the female vines nearby. Because it is clonally propagated by cuttings, 'Hercules' guarantees the sex of the plant you buy, unlike wild-collected or seed-grown stock. As with all American bittersweet, confirm nursery stock is the native Celastrus scandens and not the invasive Oriental bittersweet, Celastrus orbiculatus.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Plant container-grown rooted cuttings in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade; 'Diana' is a female-flowering American bittersweet selection that requires a nearby male pollinator such as 'Hercules' to set its showy orange-and-red fall fruit.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in moist, well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun to part shade, giving this twining native vine a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor to climb. 'Diana' is a clonally propagated female selection of American bittersweet introduced by the University of Connecticut breeding program, chosen for consistently heavy, showy fruit production once pollinated -- clusters of capsules split open in autumn to reveal bright orange-red arils that persist into winter, feeding songbirds and providing material for dried arrangements and holiday decor. Because bittersweet is dioecious, 'Diana' must be planted within pollinating range (roughly 20-30 feet) of a known male clone like 'Hercules'; without one, flowering will still occur but little or no fruit will form. Buying named female and male clones removes the guesswork of seed-grown bittersweet, where plant sex cannot be determined until flowering age. Confirm plants are the native Celastrus scandens, not the aggressively invasive Asian Celastrus orbiculatus, which has largely displaced the native species in the wild across the eastern U.S.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant small container transplants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Spetchley' is one of the smallest-leaved English ivy cultivars, growing very slowly into a dense, tight mat or miniature topiary form rather than a vigorous climber, so it is often grown in containers, troughs, or as a small-scale groundcover rather than as a wall-covering vine.

directions: Plant cuttings or small transplants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. 'Spetchley' is a dwarf, miniature-leaved sport of English ivy named for Spetchley Park in Worcestershire, England, where it originated; the tiny, dark green, lightly lobed leaves rarely exceed half an inch across, giving the plant a fine, dense, almost moss-like texture completely unlike the large-leaved common ivy. It grows extremely slowly and stays low and tight, making it a favorite for dollhouse gardens, fairy gardens, bonsai underplanting, small topiary forms, and terrarium or trough plantings rather than for covering large walls or trees. Because of its diminutive scale and slow habit, it rarely becomes invasive or weedy the way vigorous ivy cultivars can, and it tolerates close shearing to maintain a tight cushion. Give it consistent light shade and evenly moist soil for the densest growth.

common_name: Manda's Crested English Ivy (Parsley Crested Ivy)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container transplants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; 'Manda's Crested' has distinctive ruffled, wavy-edged leaves that take on bronze-purple winter color, making it a popular older cultivar for houseplant pots, hanging baskets, and shaded groundcover.

directions: Plant cuttings or transplants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. 'Manda's Crested', also widely sold as Parsley Crested ivy, is a heritage English ivy cultivar named for the W.A. Manda nursery that introduced it in the early 1900s; its small, five-lobed leaves have distinctively wavy, crinkled, crested margins that give the foliage a ruffled, parsley-like texture quite different from smooth-edged ivy. Leaves emerge medium green and shift to attractive bronze-purple tones in cold weather, adding winter interest to groundcover plantings or container displays. It is a modest, well-behaved grower compared to vigorous large-leaved ivy cultivars, making it well suited to edging, small baskets, and shaded rock garden pockets as well as traditional houseplant use. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage denser branching and fuller coverage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension -- Plants Database

common_name: Little Diamond English Ivy (Silver-Margined Dwarf Ivy)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container transplants in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade; 'Little Diamond' is a compact, slow-spreading variegated ivy with small gray-green, white-margined leaves well suited to pots, edging, and small-scale shaded groundcover rather than large-scale wall coverage.

directions: Plant cuttings or transplants in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. 'Little Diamond' is a compact, slow-growing variegated English ivy cultivar with small, diamond-shaped, gray-green leaves edged in creamy white, giving it a frosted, two-toned appearance that brightens shaded containers, window boxes, and small garden beds. Its tidy, restrained habit and slow spread make it far less likely to overrun a bed than vigorous green-leaved ivy cultivars, while still providing dense, weed-suppressing evergreen cover at a small scale. It performs equally well trailing from a hanging basket or mixed container planting and as a creeping groundcover beneath shaded shrubs. Light shade produces the best variegation contrast; deep shade can cause the white margins to fade toward plain green over time.

common_name: Jeanne Le Roux Armand Clematis (Pink-Flowered Evergreen Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade on a sturdy support; like the white-flowered species, 'Jeanne Le Roux' blooms very early on the previous year's wood, so prune lightly right after flowering if needed rather than in late winter.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade against a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence able to support a vigorous evergreen vine. 'Jeanne Le Roux' is a pink-flowered selection of the evergreen Armand clematis, bearing the same leathery, glossy, year-round foliage as the white species but with abundant clusters of soft pink, star-shaped, lightly fragrant flowers that open very early in spring, often among the first clematis to bloom. Its scent is milder than the species but still noticeable at close range, and the pink tone offers a distinct color option for gardeners wanting to echo spring-flowering shrubs like camellias or early azaleas. It grows quickly and can become large if not given room or a light post-bloom pruning to control size, since like all Armand clematis it flowers on the prior year's growth and heavy pruning at the wrong time sacrifices the coming season's display. Well suited to screening a warm, sheltered fence or arbor in mild-winter regions.

common_name: Skyland's Giant Japanese Hydrangea Vine (Extra-Large-Bracted Selection)

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil against a shaded wall, large tree, or sturdy fence in spring; 'Skyland's Giant' is selected for unusually large, oversized white bracts and, like the species, is slow to establish before becoming a vigorous climber.

directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens against a shaded wall, large tree, or fence in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil. 'Skyland's Giant' is a selection of Japanese hydrangea vine named for its exceptionally large, oversized sterile bracts -- individual heart-shaped white bracts can reach several times the size of the species' typical bloom, creating a bolder, showier lacecap-type flower display in midsummer than standard seedling plants. It attaches to surfaces by aerial rootlets exactly like the species and climbing hydrangea, remaining slow and inconspicuous for the first two to three years after planting before growing vigorously and covering large areas of shaded wall or trunk. Fall foliage turns soft yellow before leaf drop. Because flower size can vary among seedling-grown Japanese hydrangea vines, 'Skyland's Giant' is worth seeking out by name for gardeners specifically wanting the largest possible bract display on a shaded north- or east-facing wall.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants
